Rest and lying down are not the same thing.
An ache that has been building for a week gets the same prescription in every house: go and lie down. It feels like the sensible thing, and for most ordinary stiffness it is the one thing that makes the next morning worse, because a joint that has not moved for a day has not rested — it has set. Rest is doing less of the thing that caused it: fewer stairs, lighter buckets, a shorter round of the market. Rest is not doing nothing at all; slow, ordinary movement through the day is what keeps a stiff joint from becoming a stuck one. Lying down is for sleep and the half hour after lunch. And anything that swells, gives way or keeps someone awake is a question for a doctor, not a rest question.

The corner where the walk turns back.
Every regular walker has one. The temple gate, the third lamp-post, the end of the park railing. It was chosen years ago, and it has quietly moved closer to the house since, one landmark at a time, without anyone deciding it should. Two things worth doing: notice where the turn happens now and where it was a year ago, because nobody keeps this record and it is the most honest one there is. Then move it back slowly — one lamp-post further for a week before the next. The pace matters less than the turning point. A slow walk to the old corner is worth more than a brisk one to the new.

Ten minutes before the walk, not after it.
Most people reach for the jar when they come back. It also belongs before setting out: a thin layer of the soothing massage gel over the front and sides of the knees, worked in with slow strokes while sitting on the edge of the bed, is a few minutes of attention on the joints that are about to do the work — and the massage itself is half the point. It absorbs quickly and dries without leaving the skin sticky, so trousers go on straight after. Not for broken or irritated skin, nowhere near the eyes, and wash the hands afterwards. For external use only.

Colouring is handwriting practice in disguise.
Staying inside a line, changing direction without lifting the crayon, pressing lightly for a pale patch and harder for a dark one — every one of those is a writing skill, learned before a single letter is asked for. What to look for: small strokes rather than big sweeps, a crayon held nearer the tip than the end, and colour that stops at the line most of the time rather than all of the time, because perfect edges at five are a sign of tension rather than talent. If a child who hates the copybook still likes to colour, that is the practice to keep. The letters can wait a term.

When grandparents run the homework hour.
In more and more homes, the evening homework belongs to a grandparent while the parents are still on their way back. It works beautifully in some houses and badly in others, and the difference is almost never about the grandparent's education. The method has changed but the patience has not, so ask the teacher for one sheet showing how letters and sums are set out this year. Reading aloud is the thing they do best; let the reading be theirs and the corrections be the school's. The chair matters more for a seventy-year-old back than for the child. Stories count as homework. And the good page should be the one reported at the door, not the bad one. Save this post for the next time the homework hour changes hands.

If it arrives damaged, say so. That is the whole process.
Parcels travel a long way to reach most of the country, and a jar with a cracked lid or a book with a bent spine is nobody's fault at home. We would rather replace it than argue about it. Keep the parcel as it came and take one photo of the box and the item together. Send it to us with the order name through the contact page, or reply to the order message. A replacement goes out — no forms, no questions about how it happened. We ship across India, and the simplest way to be asked for a second order is to handle the first one properly.

Which household job would you retire first, if you could?
The mopping, the hand-washing, the daily trip up the stairs with the water, the bending over a low stove. Every house has one job that the back has been quietly complaining about for years, and usually one person who has been doing it without saying so. Tell us which one it is at yours in the comments, and who does it.

How to patch-test it properly, before the first full use.
Every bottle says patch-test first and almost nobody does. It takes a minute, and it is the difference between knowing and guessing on skin that has just been waxed. Where: the inside of the forearm or behind the ear — skin that is thin, easy to see, and not about to be treated. How much: one drop of Layali, worked in and left alone, with no rinsing and no covering. How long: overnight. Anything still red or itchy in the morning means it is not for you, and that is worth knowing before it goes anywhere near a freshly waxed leg. Unscented, for external use on unbroken skin.
